tagline: A mountain parks road climbs from spruce forests into alpine country
intro: The Mount Blue Sky Scenic Byway climbs more than 7,000 feet in 28 miles, leaving forest for country above timberline. On the upper road, steep grades, narrow pavement and winding turns shape the drive. The full 49-mile corridor is a Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway and a National Forest Scenic Byway. CDOT highlights its alpine lakes, wildflowers and Front Range views, and gives a driving time of two hours.

Denver Mountain Parks planned the road to connect Echo Lake and Summit Lake with its lower foothill parks. Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. set the route, with scenic views part of the plan from the beginning. Construction reached Echo Lake in 1921; the final 600 feet of the summit road were built by hand and completed in 1930. The original plan approached Echo Lake from Bergen Park before climbing to the summit; the road down Chicago Creek Canyon was a secondary branch.

From Idaho Springs, follow Highway 103 to Echo Lake, then Highway 5 toward the summit. The climb passes Mount Goliath and Summit Lake before ending at a parking area just below the peak. The wider corridor also extends east from Echo Lake to Bergen Park on Clear Creek County Road 103 and Jefferson County Road 66.

moments.title: Echo Lake
moments.text: Echo Lake owes its basin to retreating ice: glacial moraines blocked drainage in the Chicago Creek valley and formed a natural dam. The shallow lake lies at 10,600 feet, among Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir. Its park belongs to the Denver Mountain Parks system. At one end is a stone picnic shelter; at the other is Echo Lake Lodge, built in 1926. Architect Jacques Benedict gave the lodge two octagonal log stories on a base of local granite. Outside the lodge, a historic plaque commemorates cosmic-ray experiments conducted at the lake and on the mountain between 1935 and 1960.

moments.title: Summit Lake
moments.text: Summit Lake sits in a glacial cirque on the north face of Mount Blue Sky and the east face of Mount Spalding. At 12,836 feet, this lake is the headwaters of Bear Creek. Permafrost east of the water helps prevent drainage, and the park contains alpine tundra. Denver acquired the land in 1924 and brought it into the Mountain Parks system. In April 1965, it became a National Natural Landmark. North of the lake, a saddle looks down toward the two cirques holding the Chicago Lakes, at the headwaters of a different stream, Chicago Creek.

moments.title: Mount Blue Sky
moments.text: The summit road gave researchers access to high-altitude experiments as well as mountain views. Arthur H. Compton studied cosmic rays here in 1931, shortly after the road was completed. The University of Denver built two A-frame buildings to house researchers. In 1939, Bruno Rossi used sites at Mount Blue Sky, Echo Lake, Denver and Chicago to measure the lifetime of the muon. Another summit structure met a different end: Crest House burned in 1979 and was never rebuilt. Its rock foundation and walls remain, serving as a windbreak for mountain travelers.

practical: Mount Blue Sky: The summit road is seasonal. CDOT lists Memorial Day through Labor Day for summit access and requires vehicle reservations. (checked 2026-10-11)
